title: Impact of extraction methods on the properties of Carica papaya pseudostem fibers from Cameroon used as reinforcement in

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states Cameroon 'ranks 64th in the world in papaya production, with an annual output of 44 tons.' A national annual papaya output of only 44 tons is implausibly low by orders of magnitude and is almost certainly wrong or missing a unit prefix such as 'thousand tonnes.'

The abstract claims FTIR shows 'cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin functional groups ... are dissolved considerably as the percentage of NaOH increases,' and the Introduction says alkaline treatment dissolves 'cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and pectin.' Cellulose is not appreciably dissolved by 2.5–7.5% NaOH; alkaline extraction mainly removes hemicellulose and lignin, so the claim is chemically wrong.

The text states 'A decrease of 302.02 ± 4 μm for fibers extracted by water retting and 196.33 ± 4 μm - 221.94 ± 6 μm - 219.31 ± 4 μm respectively...' This describes diameter values as a 'decrease,' which is nonsensical as written. Also, the NaOH series is not monotonic (2.5% gives the smallest mean diameter, 5% gives the largest among NaOH treatments), yet the text attributes the results to NaOH causing narrowing of diameters.
The tensile modulus is reported as '8.271 ± 1.62' with no units. A modulus must have units (e.g., GPa or MPa); as written the value is scientifically incomplete and uninterpretable.

The FTIR and TGA methods state that samples were ground to 'a size of 0.3 μm' or prepared as 'powder (0.3 μm).' A particle size of 0.3 μm is unrealistic for routine grinding of lignocellulosic fibers and is likely a unit error for 0.3 mm.

In water retting (2.2), fibers are 'sun-dried for 24 h to remove moisture,' but in chemical extraction (2.3) it says 'The fibers extracted by the different techniques were dried at 28 °C in the sun for 72 h,' including water-retted fibers. The drying duration for water-retted fibers is therefore inconsistent (24 h vs 72 h).
The text defines Young's modulus as 'the linear part of the stress-strain curve.' Young's modulus is the slope of the initial linear region of the stress-strain curve, not the linear part itself.

The FTIR instrument is described as a 'Shimadzu IRAffinity⁻¹ CE' controlled by 'Opus/Mentor software.' Opus is Bruker Optics software, not Shimadzu FTIR software, so the software attribution is likely incorrect.
